claim: Eukaryotic DNA replication initiates during S phase from origins that have been licensed in the preceding G1 phase.
source: Eukaryotic DNA replication initiates during S phase from origins that have been licensed in the preceding G1 phase.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive literature and represents foundational knowledge in the field.

claim: Both the origin recognition complex (ORC) and the minichromosome maintenance complex (MCM) are significantly and homogeneously depleted from transcribed genes.
source: Both, the origin recognition complex (ORC) and the minichromosome maintenance complex (MCM) are significantly and homogeneously depleted from transcribed genes, enriched at gene promoters, and more abundant in early- than in late-replicating domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript showing ORC/MCM distributions relative to transcribed genes.

claim: ORC and MCM are enriched at gene promoters.
source: Both, the origin recognition complex (ORC) and the minichromosome maintenance complex (MCM) are significantly and homogeneously depleted from transcribed genes, enriched at gene promoters, and more abundant in early- than in late-replicating domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq analysis showing enrichment at transcription start sites (TSSs).

claim: ORC and MCM are more abundant in early- than in late-replicating domains.
source: Both, the origin recognition complex (ORC) and the minichromosome maintenance complex (MCM) are significantly and homogeneously depleted from transcribed genes, enriched at gene promoters, and more abundant in early- than in late-replicating domains.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ChIP-seq data with Repli-seq replication timing data.

claim: After controlling for replication timing and transcription variables, no difference in ORC/MCM density is detected between initiation zones, termination zones, unidirectionally replicating regions, and randomly replicating regions.
source: Surprisingly, after controlling these variables, no difference in ORC/MCM density is detected between initiation zones, termination zones, unidirectionally replicating regions, and randomly replicating regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data across different replication fork directionality patterns.

claim: ORC/MCM density correlates with replication timing but does not solely regulate the probability of replication initiation.
source: Therefore, ORC/MCM density correlates with replication timing but does not solely regulate the probability of replication initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density does not distinguish initiation zones from other regions of similar replication timing.

claim: H4K20me3 was enriched in late-replicating initiation zones and gene deserts of stochastic replication fork direction.
source: Interestingly, H4K20me3, a histone modification proposed to facilitate late origin licensing, was enriched in late-replicating initiation zones and gene deserts of stochastic replication fork direction.
evidence: This is supported by H4K20me3 ChIP-seq data analyzed in relation to OK-seq replication fork directionality data.

claim: In human cells, DNA replication initiates from 20,000 to 50,000 replication origins selected from a five- to tenfold excess of potential or 'licensed' origins.
source: In human cells, DNA replication initiates from 20,000 to 50,000 replication origins selected from a five- to tenfold excess of potential or 'licensed' origins (Moiseeva and Bakkenist, 2018; Papior et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Origin licensing occurs in late mitosis and during the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Origin licensing, also called pre-replicative complex (pre-RC) formation, occurs in late mitosis and during the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cell cycle regulation.

claim: During origin licensing, the origin recognition complex (ORC) binds DNA and, together with Cdt1 and Cdc6, loads minichromosome maintenance complexes (MCM) as inactive head-to-head double hexamers around double-stranded DNA.
source: During this step, the origin recognition complex (ORC) binds DNA and, together with Cdt1 and Cdc6, loads minichromosome maintenance complexes (MCM), the core motor of the replicative helicase, as inactive head-to-head double hexamers (MCM-DHs) around double-stranded DNA (Bell and Kaguni, 2013; Evrin et al., 2009; Remus and Diffley, 2009).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: A single ORC reiteratively loads multiple MCM-DHs.
source: A single ORC reiteratively loads multiple MCM-DHs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of origin licensing.

claim: Once MCM-DHs have been assembled, ORC does not maintain contact with the MCM-DH.
source: However, once MCM-DHs have been assembled, ORC does not maintain contact with the MCM-DH and neither ORC, nor Cdc6, nor Cdt1 are required for origin activation (Fragkos et al., 2015; Hyrien, 2016; Powell et al., 2015; Remus et al., 2009; Rowles et al., 1999; Sun et al., 2014; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Neither ORC, nor Cdc6, nor Cdt1 are required for origin activation.
source: However, once MCM-DHs have been assembled, ORC does not maintain contact with the MCM-DH and neither ORC, nor Cdc6, nor Cdt1 are required for origin activation (Fragkos et al., 2015; Hyrien, 2016; Powell et al., 2015; Remus et al., 2009; Rowles et al., 1999; Sun et al., 2014; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: During S phase, CDK2 and CDC7 kinase activities in conjunction with other origin-firing factors convert some MCM-DHs into pairs of active CDC45-MCM-GINS helicases that nucleate bidirectional replisome establishment.
source: During S phase, CDK2 and CDC7 kinase activities in conjunction with other origin-firing factors convert some MCM-DHs into pairs of active CDC45-MCM-GINS helicases that nucleate bidirectional replisome establishment (Douglas et al., 2018; Moiseeva and Bakkenist, 2018).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by cited studies.

claim: MCM-DHs that do not initiate replication are dislodged from DNA during replication.
source: MCM-DHs that do not initiate replication are dislodged from DNA during replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCM-DH dynamics during replication.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, origins are genetically defined by specific DNA sequences.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, origins are genetically defined by specific DNA sequences (Marahrens and Stillman, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: In multicellular organisms, no consensus sequence for origin activity has been identified and replication initiates from flexible locations.
source: In multicellular organisms, no consensus sequence for origin activity has been identified and replication initiates from flexible locations.
evidence: This is established knowledge contrasting yeast with metazoan replication origins.

claim: Mammalian origins fire at different times through S phase, and neighboring origins tend to fire at similar times, partitioning the genome into ~5,000 replication timing domains (RTDs).
source: Although mammalian origins fire at different times through S phase, neighboring origins tend to fire at similar times, partitioning the genome into ~5,000 replication timing domains (RTDs) (Rivera-Mulia and Gilbert, 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: RTDs replicate in a reproducible order through S phase.
source: RTDs replicate in a reproducible order through S phase (Pope et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: One model for temporal regulation of replication suggests that RTDs are first selected for initiation, followed by stochastic origin firing within domains.
source: One model for this temporal regulation suggests that RTDs are first selected for initiation, followed by stochastic origin firing within domains (Boulos et al., 2015; Pope et al., 2014; Rhind and Gilbert, 2013; Rivera-Mulia and Gilbert, 2016b).
evidence: This model is supported by cited studies.

claim: A cascade or domino model suggests that replication first initiates at the most efficient (master) origins and then spreads to less efficient origins within an RTD.
source: A cascade or domino model suggests that replication first initiates at the most efficient (master) origins and then spreads to less efficient origins within an RTD (Boos and Ferreira, 2019; Guilbaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This alternative model is supported by cited studies.

claim: Various processes and factors contribute to origin specification such as transcription, DNA sequences, histone variants, histone modifications, and nucleosome dynamics.
source: Various processes and factors contribute to origin specification such as transcription, DNA sequences, histone variants, histone modifications, and nucleosome dynamics (Akerman et al., 2020; Cayrou et al., 2015; Long et al., 2020; Petryk et al., 2016; Prioleau and MacAlpine, 2016; Smith and Aladjem, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: H4K20me3 supports the licensing of a subset of late-replicating origins in heterochromatin.
source: For example, we proposed H4K20me3 to support the licensing of a subset of late-replicating origins in heterochromatin (Brustel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study from the authors' group.

claim: The histone variant H2A.Z has been implicated in ORC recruitment at early origins through deposition of H4K20me2 by histone methyltransferase SUV420H1.
source: Recently, the histone variant H2A.Z has been implicated in ORC recruitment at early origins through deposition of H4K20me2 by histone methyltransferase SUV420H1 (Long et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Binding sites for the origin-firing factor Treslin-MTBP often feature a nucleosome-free gap adjacent to H3K4me2.
source: Furthermore, binding sites for the origin-firing factor Treslin-MTBP often feature a nucleosome-free gap adjacent to H3K4me2 (Kumagai and Dunphy, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: OK-seq reveals the population-averaged replication fork direction (RFD) allowing to map initiation and termination.
source: Strand-oriented sequencing of Okazaki fragments (OK-seq) reveals the population-averaged replication fork direction (RFD) allowing to map initiation and termination (Chen et al., 2019; McGuffee et al., 2013; Petryk et al., 2016; Smith and Whitehouse, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies describing the OK-seq method.

claim: Bubble-seq, single-molecule analyses, and OK-seq studies of human cells all suggest that replication initiates in broad but circumscribed zones consisting of multiple, individually inefficient sites.
source: Bubble-seq (Mesner et al., 2013), single-molecule analyses (Demczuk et al., 2012; Lebofsky et al., 2006; Norio et al., 2005), and OK-seq (Petryk et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018) studies of human cells all suggest that replication initiates in broad but circumscribed zones consisting of multiple, individually inefficient sites.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies using different methodologies.

claim: OK-seq revealed both early-firing initiation zones (IZs), which are precisely flanked on one or both sides by actively transcribed genes, and late-firing IZs distantly located from active genes.
source: OK-seq revealed both, early-firing initiation zones (IZs), which are precisely flanked on one or both sides by actively transcribed genes, and late-firing IZs distantly located from active genes (Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: An excellent agreement was observed between early-firing IZs determined by OK-seq and by EdUseq-HU.
source: Recently, an excellent agreement was observed between early-firing IZs determined by OK-seq and by EdUseq-HU, which identifies nascent DNA synthesized in early S phase cells in the presence of EdU and hydroxyurea (Tubbs et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: High-resolution Repli-seq identified both early and late IZs consistent with OK-seq IZs.
source: Furthermore, high-resolution Repli-seq identified both early and late IZs consistent with OK-seq IZs (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: In Drosophila, ORC often binds next to open chromatin marks found at transcription start sites (TSSs).
source: In Drosophila, ORC often binds next to open chromatin marks found at transcription start sites (TSSs) (MacAlpine et al., 2010), but MCMs, initially loaded next to ORC, are more abundantly loaded and widely redistributed when cyclin E/CDK2 activity rises in late G1 (Powell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: In Drosophila, MCMs, initially loaded next to ORC, are more abundantly loaded and widely redistributed when cyclin E/CDK2 activity rises in late G1.
source: In Drosophila, ORC often binds next to open chromatin marks found at transcription start sites (TSSs) (MacAlpine et al., 2010), but MCMs, initially loaded next to ORC, are more abundantly loaded and widely redistributed when cyclin E/CDK2 activity rises in late G1 (Powell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: ChIP-seq of single ORC subunits identified from 13,000 to 101,000 ORC potential binding sites in human cells.
source: In human cells, ChIP-seq of single ORC subunits identified from 13,000 to 101,000 ORC potential binding sites (Dellino et al., 2013; Long et al., 2020; Miotto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: ChIP-seq of Mcm7 in HeLa cells suggested that MCM-DHs bind regardless of the chromatin environment, but are preferentially activated upstream of active TSSs.
source: ChIP-seq of Mcm7 in HeLa cells suggested that MCM-DHs bind regardless of the chromatin environment, but are preferentially activated upstream of active TSSs (Sugimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: A five- to tenfold excess of potential origins were licensed per EBV genome with respect to 1–3 mapped initiation event(s).
source: A five- to tenfold excess of potential origins were licensed per genome with respect to 1–3 mapped initiation event(s) (Norio, 2001; Norio and Schildkraut, 2004; Papior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies using EBV as a model system.

claim: ChIP efficiencies and qualities were measured using the EBV latent origin oriP as reference.
source: ChIP efficiencies and qualities were measured using the EBV latent origin oriP as reference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Raji cells contain 50–60 EBV episomes, allowing an easy detection of ORC/MCM at oriP.
source: Raji cells contain 50–60 EBV episomes, allowing an easy detection of ORC/MCM at oriP (Adams et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The viral protein EBNA1 recruits ORC to oriP's dyad symmetry element, followed by MCM-DH loading.
source: The viral protein EBNA1 recruits ORC to oriP's dyad symmetry element, followed by MCM-DH loading.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EBV replication.

claim: Both ORC and MCM were detected at the dyad symmetry element in G1, whereas a population containing S-G2-M-phased cells depicted a reduction in MCM levels.
source: We detected both ORC and MCM at the dyad symmetry element in G1, whereas a population containing S-G2-M-phased cells depict a reduction in MCM levels, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c; Papior et al., 2012; Ritzi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in the referenced figure and supported by cited studies.

claim: ChIP-seq of two replicates for ORC subunits (Orc2, Orc3) and of three replicates for MCM proteins (Mcm3, Mcm7) resulted in reproducible, but dispersed, ChIP-seq signals.
source: ChIP-seq of two replicates for ORC subunits (Orc2, Orc3) and of three replicates for MCM proteins (Mcm3, Mcm7) resulted in reproducible, but dispersed, ChIP-seq signals as exemplified by the well-characterized replication origin Mcm4/PRKDC (Figure 1a; Ladenburger et al., 2002; Schaarschmidt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The input control was significantly underrepresented in DNase hypersensitive (HS) regions, at TSSs, and at early RTDs.
source: In line with a previous report (Teytelman et al., 2009), the input control was significantly underrepresented in DNase hypersensitive (HS) regions, at TSSs, and at early RTDs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in the referenced figure and supported by a cited study.

claim: Sonication-hypersensitive regions correlate with DNase HS regions.
source: As sonication-hypersensitive regions correlate with DNase HS regions (Schwartz et al., 2005), we carefully compared our results obtained with and without input normalization.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 is r = 0.866.
source: The reliability and reproducibility of our ChIP experiments is reflected by the high Pearson correlation coefficients of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 (r = 0.866, Figure 1c) and Mcm3/Mcm7 (r = 0.879, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation plot shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient of the relative read frequencies of Mcm3/Mcm7 is r = 0.879.
source: The reliability and reproducibility of our ChIP experiments is reflected by the high Pearson correlation coefficients of the relative read frequencies of Orc2/Orc3 (r = 0.866, Figure 1c) and Mcm3/Mcm7 (r = 0.879, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation plot shown in Figure 1d.

claim: ORC ChIP-seq data shows substantial enrichment around K562 Orc2 peaks.
source: To compare our ChIP-seq data to previously published Orc2 ChIP-seq from asynchronously cycling K562 cells (GSE70165; Miotto et al., 2016), we calculated the relative read frequencies of our ORC ChIPs around an aggregate of K562 Orc2 peaks (>1 kb) and found substantial enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Orc2 co-localizes with DNase HS sites present at active promoters and enhancers.
source: Miotto et al., 2016 reported that Orc2 co-localizes with DNase HS sites present at active promoters and enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of ORC at DNase HS regions > 1 kb, compared to regions deprived of DNase HS sites.
source: In line with these observations, we found a significant enrichment of ORC at DNase HS regions > 1 kb, compared to regions deprived of DNase HS sites, with or without input normalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f, g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 2957 ascending segments (ASs) with an average size of 52.3 kb were selected, covering 4.9% (155 Mb) of the genome.
source: In total, we selected 2957 ASs, with an average size of 52.3 kb, which covered 4.9% (155 Mb) of the genome (Figure 2a, green bars, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the OK-seq analysis and summarized in Table 1.

claim: 2451 (83%) of all AS located close to genic regions.
source: In total, 2451 (83%) of all AS located close to genic regions (ASs extended by 20 kb on both sides overlapped with at least one annotated gene).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AS positions relative to annotated genes.

claim: 673 ASs (22.8% of all ASs) were flanked by actively transcribed genes on both sides (type 1 AS).
source: Performing RNA-seq in asynchronously cycling Raji cells, we determined that 673 ASs (22.8% of all ASs) were flanked by actively transcribed genes (transcripts per kilobase per million [TPM] >3) on both sides (type 1 AS), with less than 20 kb between AS borders and the closest transcribed gene.
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 1026 ASs (34.7%) had only one border associated to a transcribed gene (type 2 AS).
source: In total, 1026 ASs (34.7%) had only one border associated to a transcribed gene (type 2 AS; TPM >3).
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 506 ASs (17.1%) were devoid of proximal genes (non-genic AS).
source: Also, 506 ASs (17.1%) were devoid of proximal genes (non-genic AS) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on combined analysis of OK-seq and gene annotation data.

claim: Type 1 ASs were on average slightly more efficient than type 2 ASs, followed by non-genic ASs.
source: The slope did not change considerably between the different AS types, although type 1 ASs were on average slightly more efficient, followed by type 2 ASs, then non-genic ASs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of RFD slopes shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Type 1 and 2 ASs located within early RTDs, while non-genic ASs were predominantly late replicating.
source: Type 1 and 2 ASs located within early RTDs, while non-genic ASs were predominantly late replicating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), as previously observed in GM06990 and HeLa (Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in the referenced figure and supported by a cited study.

claim: Both ORC and MCM were, on average, enriched within ASs compared to flanking regions.
source: Both ORC and MCM were, on average, enriched within ASs compared to flanking regions (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a without input division).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the aggregate analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Transcriptional activity in AS flanking regions was associated with increased ORC/MCM levels inside ASs and a prominent MCM depletion from transcribed regions.
source: Transcriptional activity in AS flanking regions was associated with increased ORC/MCM levels inside ASs (compare Figure 2b, c) and a prominent MCM depletion from transcribed regions (Figure 2c, d, right border).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of different AS types shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In type 2 ASs, ORC/MCM levels remained elevated at non-transcribed AS borders.
source: In contrast, in type 2 ASs, ORC/MCM levels remained elevated at non-transcribed AS borders (Figure 2d, left border).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: No ORC/MCM enrichment was detected within non-genic ASs.
source: No ORC/MCM enrichment was detected within non-genic ASs (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: AS borders associated with transcriptional activity were locally enriched in ORC/MCM.
source: AS borders associated with transcriptional activity were locally enriched in ORC/MCM (Figure 2c, d, both and right borders respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: Orc1 accumulation at AS borders was previously detected.
source: This is in line with previously detected Orc1 accumulation at AS borders (Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Non-genic AS borders only showed a local dip in ORC/MCM levels.
source: Reciprocally, non-genic AS borders only showed a local dip in ORC/MCM levels (Figure 2d, left border; Figure 2e, both borders), but the biological significance of this observation remains unclear.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The average RFD profile of active genes revealed strong ASs upstream of TSSs and downstream of transcriptional termination site (TTSs), and descending RFD segments (DSs) across the active gene bodies.
source: Consistent with previous OK-seq studies (Chen et al., 2019; Petryk et al., 2016), the average RFD profile of active genes revealed strong ASs upstream of TSSs and downstream of transcriptional termination site (TTSs), and descending RFD segments (DSs) across the active gene bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure and supported by cited studies.

claim: Silent genes displayed an overall flat RFD profile.
source: This behavior depended on transcriptional activity as silent genes displayed an overall flat RFD profile (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The ORC relative read distribution was significantly enriched at active TSSs.
source: When setting our ORC/MCM ChIP-seq data in relation to transcription, we observed that the ORC relative read distribution was significantly enriched at active TSSs, as already demonstrated in Drosophila (MacAlpine et al., 2010) and human cells (Dellino et al., 2013; Miotto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq analysis and supported by cited studies.

claim: ORC relative read distribution was moderately but significantly higher upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs than within active genes.
source: Thereby, ORC relative read distribution was moderately but significantly higher upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs than within active genes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The depletion of ORC from gene bodies was statistically significant for approximately 45% of actively transcribed genes.
source: The depletion of ORC from gene bodies was statistically significant for approximately 45% of actively transcribed genes (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced.
source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 75% of investigated transcribed gene bodies were significantly depleted from Mcm3.
source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies were significantly depleted from Mcm7.
source: Compared to ORC, Mcm3 and Mcm7 enrichments at TSSs were less prominent, but depletions from gene bodies were more pronounced (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), with 75% and 58% of investigated transcribed gene bodies significantly depleted from Mcm3 and Mcm7, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Depletion of ORC/MCM from gene bodies was strictly homogeneous from TSS to TTS, strongly suggesting that transcription itself displaces ORC and MCM-DH complexes.
source: Depletion was strictly homogeneous from TSS to TTS, strongly suggesting that transcription itself displaces ORC and MCM-DH complexes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is inferred from the uniform depletion pattern observed across gene bodies.

claim: At silent genes, ORC/MCM were hardly enriched at TSSs and were not depleted from gene bodies.
source: In contrast, at silent genes, ORC/MCM were hardly enriched at TSSs and were not depleted from gene bodies (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Increasing transcriptional activity did not have any major impact on ORC/MCM enrichments at TSSs.
source: Increasing transcriptional activity (classified as low: 3–10 TPM; mid: 10–40 TPM; high:>40 TPM) did not have any major impact on ORC/MCM enrichments at TSSs (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: ORC/MCM depletion within gene bodies was slightly more pronounced with increasing transcription levels when normalized for input.
source: ORC/MCM depletion within gene bodies was slightly more pronounced with increasing transcription levels when normalized for input (Figure 3d), but this was less convincing without input normalization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Basal ORC/MCM levels upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs were identical.
source: Basal ORC/MCM levels upstream of TSSs and downstream of TTSs were identical, indicating that the local ORC enrichment at TSSs did not result in more MCM loading upstream than downstream of active genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ChIP-seq signals upstream and downstream of genes.

claim: The observation that Mcm3 and Mcm7 are significantly depleted from transcribed gene bodies is consistent with their active displacement by transcription in G1.
source: Our observation that Mcm3 and Mcm7 are significantly depleted from transcribed gene bodies is consistent with their active displacement by transcription in G1, as previously proposed in Drosophila (Powell et al., 2015) and human cells (Macheret and Halazonetis, 2018).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by cited studies in other systems.

claim: The depletion of MCM from transcribed genes contributes to delineating IZs flanked by active genes.
source: This depletion process contributes to delineating IZs flanked by active genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MCM depletion from genes creates boundaries for initiation zones.

claim: ORC/MCM density remained constant across non-genic AS borders, suggesting that ORC/MCM are not sufficient to delimit non-genic replication IZs.
source: In contrast, ORC/MCM density remained constant across non-genic AS borders (Figure 2), suggesting that ORC/MCM are not sufficient to delimit non-genic replication IZs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ORC/MCM enrichment at non-genic AS borders.

claim: In yeast, the number of MCM-DHs loaded at origins correlates with RT.
source: In yeast, it has been reported that the number of MCM-DHs loaded at origins correlates with RT, suggesting how RT profiles can emerge from stochastic origin firing (Das et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies in yeast.

claim: In human cells, ORC binding data have been used to predict RT profiles.
source: In human cells, ORC binding data have also been used to predict RT profiles (Miotto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Expressed genes showed lower ORC/MCM densities than silent genes and intergenic regions.
source: Consistently with Figure 3a, b, expressed genes showed lower ORC/MCM densities than silent genes and intergenic regions (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d, e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The difference in ORC/MCM density between expressed genes and intergenic regions was particularly significant in early- and mid-replicating regions.
source: This was particularly significant in early- and mid-replicating regions, as demonstrated by Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, red circles).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The depletion of MCM from expressed genes was more pronounced than for ORC.
source: The depletion was more pronounced for MCM than ORC, as already noted in Figure 3a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ORC and MCM ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The difference between silent genes and intergenic regions in ORC/MCM density was at best marginally significant.
source: In contrast, the difference between silent genes and intergenic regions was at best marginally significant (blue circles).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis.

claim: ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows.
source: In all cases, ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows, but this RT dependency was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM, as expected if transcription removes this complex from both early- and late-replicating genes (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The RT dependency of ORC/MCM density was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM.
source: In all cases, ORC/MCM densities monotonously decreased from early to late RT windows, but this RT dependency was much attenuated in expressed genes, particularly for MCM, as expected if transcription removes this complex from both early- and late-replicating genes (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 2D histogram analysis and is consistent with transcription-mediated removal of MCM.

claim: The analysis did not reveal any clear differences in the levels of ORC/MCM between intergenic ASs, DSs, URRs, and NRRs when bins of similar RT were compared.
source: Strikingly, our analysis did not reveal any clear differences in the levels of ORC/MCM between intergenic ASs, DSs, URRs, and NRRs when bins of similar RT were compared (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistical analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The densities of ORC/MCM across genomic segments were related to RT and gene expression but were not predictive of any RFD pattern.
source: In summary, the densities of ORC/MCM across genomic segments were related to RT and gene expression but were not predictive of any RFD pattern.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis showing no correlation between ORC/MCM density and RFD patterns after controlling for RT and transcription.

claim: The slope of an RFD segment is proportional to the difference between the density of initiation and termination events within the segment.
source: Strictly speaking, the slope of an RFD segment is proportional to the difference between the density of initiation and termination events within the segment (Audit et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study describing the mathematical relationship.

claim: Initiation events within URRs can almost certainly be excluded.
source: In contrast, we can almost certainly exclude initiation events within URRs, but their ORC/MCM densities were not significantly lower than in ASs.
evidence: This is inferred from the definition of URRs as unidirectionally replicating regions.

claim: Specific mechanisms repress potential origins in URRs and/or activate them in ASs.
source: This suggests that specific mechanisms repress potential origins in URRs and/or activate them in ASs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that URRs have similar ORC/MCM density to ASs but do not initiate replication.

claim: The density of ORC/MCM is not a reliable predictor of initiation probability, even though ORC density well correlated with RT.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the density of ORC/MCM is not a reliable predictor of initiation probability, even though ORC density (and to a lesser extent MCM density) well correlated with RT.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of ORC/MCM density relative to replication initiation and timing.

claim: Potential origins are widespread through the genome, but additional genetic or epigenetic factors are regulating whether and when they fire.
source: Thus, potential origins are widespread through the genome, but additional genetic or epigenetic factors are regulating whether and when they fire.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density does not predict initiation sites.

claim: 302 early RTDs covering 642.8 Mb and 287 late RTDs covering 617.4 Mb of the genome were extracted.
source: To confirm this observation, we extracted early and late RTDs employing a threshold of log2(Early/Late) > 1.6 for early RTDs and <−2.0 for late RTDs, which resulted in 302 early RTDs covering 642.8 Mb and 287 late RTDs covering 617.4 Mb of the genome.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Repli-seq data.

claim: ORC was 1.4 times enriched in early RTDs compared to late RTDs.
source: ORC was 1.4 times enriched in early RTDs compared to late RTDs (Figure 5a, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures and table.

claim: Mcm3 and Mcm7 levels showed the same tendencies as ORC but were less contrasted.
source: Mcm3 and Mcm7 levels, although showing the same tendencies, were less contrasted than ORC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of ChIP-seq signals in early versus late RTDs.

claim: In S-G2-M chromatin, ORC was still significantly enriched in early RTDs, compared to late RTDs, but MCMs were not.
source: In S-G2-M chromatin, ORC was still significantly enriched in early RTDs, compared to late RTDs, but MCMs were not, consistent with completed replication of early but not late RTDs (Figure 5b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures and is consistent with MCM displacement during replication.

claim: The MCM signal is dynamic through the cell cycle.
source: These results demonstrate that the MCM signal is dynamic through the cell cycle as expected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of G1 and S-G2-M chromatin.

claim: The preferential binding of ORC to early replicating (open) chromatin is not dependent on cell cycle stage.
source: These results also show that the preferential binding of ORC to early replicating (open) chromatin is not dependent on cell cycle stage.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the persistence of ORC enrichment in early RTDs in S-G2-M chromatin.

claim: Orc1 in human cells is degraded at the G1-S transition and in early S phase.
source: Given that Orc1 in human cells is degraded at the G1-S transition and in early S phase (Kreitz et al., 2001; Méndez et al., 2002; Ohta et al., 2003), it might appear surprising that we detect Orc2 and Orc3 binding to S-G2-M chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Orc1 reappears as cells enter mitosis and is the first ORC subunit to bind to mitotic chromosomes, but other ORC subunits seem to join only in daughter G1 cells.
source: In human cells, Orc1 reappears as cells enter mitosis and is the first ORC subunit to bind to mitotic chromosomes, but other ORC subunits seem to join only in daughter G1 cells (Kara et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: GFP‐tagged Orc1 was found to associate with chromatin throughout mitosis in living Chinese hamster cells and to co-localize with Orc4 in metaphase spreads.
source: Nevertheless, GFP‐tagged Orc1 was found to associate with chromatin throughout mitosis in living Chinese hamster cells and to co-localize with Orc4 in metaphase spreads (Okuno et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The binding of Orc2 and Orc3 detected in S-G2-M may either occur independently of Orc1 or reflect the binding of the entire complex in late mitotic cells.
source: The binding of Orc2 and Orc3 we detect in S-G2-M may either occur independently of Orc1 or reflect the binding of the entire complex in late mitotic cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of ORC binding in S-G2-M.

claim: H4K20me3 is involved in licensing a subset of late-replicating regions.
source: We and others recently demonstrated that H4K20me3 is involved in licensing a subset of late-replicating regions (Benetti et al., 2007; Brustel et al., 2017; Pannetier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies including work from the authors' group.

claim: ORC and, to a lower extent, MCM were enriched at H4K20me3 peaks.
source: We calculated ORC/MCM relative read frequencies binned at 1 kb resolution at H4K20me3/H4K20me1 peaks > 1 kb (12,251 and 6277 peaks, respectively). ORC and, to a lower extent, MCM were enriched at H4K20me3, but not H4K20me1 peaks (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: H4K20me3 coverage at the different AS types depicts an increased H4K20me3 signal only in non-genic ASs.
source: H4K20me3 coverage at the different AS types depicts an increased H4K20me3 signal only in non-genic ASs, disclosing the first histone modification specific for late-replicating non-genic ASs (Figure 5d, e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figures 5d and 5e.

claim: ORC/MCM were enriched at the H4K20me3-high subgroup of non-genic ASs compared to the H4K20me3-low subgroup.
source: Starting from 506 non-genic ASs, we extracted two subsets of 154 and 242 non-genic ASs, where H4K20me3 relative read frequencies were above the mean genome value by more than 1.5× standard deviation, or below the genome mean value, respectively. ORC/MCM were enriched at the H4K20me3-high subgroup compared to the H4K20me3-low subgroup (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The presence of H4K20me3 at transcriptionally independent, non-genic ASs may contribute at the origin-licensing step to specifying these regions as highly efficient 'master' initiation zones (Ma-IZs) in late-replicating DNA.
source: These results suggest that the presence of H4K20me3 at transcriptionally independent, non-genic ASs may contribute at the origin-licensing step to specifying these regions as highly efficient 'master' initiation zones (Ma-IZs) in late-replicating DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of ORC/MCM at H4K20me3-high non-genic ASs.

claim: The difference of ORC/MCM densities between H4K20me3-high and -low subgroups was less pronounced in chromatin derived from S-G2-M-phased cells.
source: The difference of ORC/MCM densities between H4K20me3-high and -low subgroups was less pronounced in chromatin derived from S-G2-M-phased cells. The dynamic differences between the cell cycle fractions confirm the biological relevance of this finding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The H4K20me3 level was weakly but systematically more abundant in early than in late-replicating chromatin.
source: First, the H4K20me3 level was weakly but systematically more abundant in early than in late-replicating chromatin, suggesting that H4K20me3 is not exclusively present in late-replicating heterochromatin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 2D histogram analysis of H4K20me3 versus RT.

claim: H4K20me3 is not exclusively present in late-replicating heterochromatin.
source: First, the H4K20me3 level was weakly but systematically more abundant in early than in late-replicating chromatin, suggesting that H4K20me3 is not exclusively present in late-replicating heterochromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H4K20me3 is more abundant in early-replicating chromatin.

claim: The H4K20me3 level was slightly lower in transcribed genes than in the non-transcribed rest of the genome.
source: Second, the H4K20me3 level was slightly lower in transcribed genes than in the non-transcribed rest of the genome (Figure 6a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AS and DS bins showed comparable distributions of H4K20me3 levels at comparable RT and gene expression status.
source: Third, AS and DS bins showed comparable distributions of H4K20me3 levels at comparable RT and gene expression status (Figure 6a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: NRRs showed a specific, broader distribution of H4K20me3 levels, including a higher proportion of highly enriched windows, especially compared to URRs.
source: Interestingly, NRRs showed a specific, broader distribution of H4K20me3 levels, including a higher proportion of highly enriched windows, especially compared to URRs (compare boxplots in Figure 6a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Locally, high densities of H4K20me3 are detected in late, non-genic AS segments and in late-replicating gene deserts of null RFD.
source: Locally, high densities of H4K20me3 are therefore detected not only in late, non-genic AS segments but also in late-replicating gene deserts of null RFD, which presumably replicate by widespread, spatially random initiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis of H4K20me3 distribution in different genomic regions.

claim: ORC/MCM were more abundant at H4K20me3-high than -low bins in NRRs.
source: This result led us to repeat the analysis of ORC/MCM enrichment at H4K20me3-high and -low 10 kb intergenic bins in NRRs. Again, ORC/MCM were more abundant at H4K20me3-high than -low bins (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: H4K20me3 facilitates origin licensing specifically in heterochromatic segments.
source: These findings support the hypothesis that H4K20me3 facilitates origin licensing specifically in these heterochromatic segments (Brustel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of ORC/MCM at H4K20me3-high regions and supported by a cited study.

claim: The entire genome (except transcribed genes) is licensed for replication initiation.
source: These findings support the cascade model for replication initiation: the entire genome (except transcribed genes) is licensed for replication initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread distribution of ORC/MCM throughout the genome except in transcribed genes.

claim: Additional process and factors like adjacent active transcription and epigenetic marks are required to specify master zones of higher replication initiation efficiency.
source: Additional process and factors like adjacent active transcription and epigenetic marks are required to specify master zones of higher replication initiation efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density alone does not predict initiation zones.

claim: The distributed licensing pattern allows the stochastic activation of secondary origins, possibly triggered by approaching replication forks.
source: The distributed licensing pattern allows the stochastic activation of secondary origins, possibly triggered by approaching replication forks.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of secondary origin activation.

claim: Transcription has both positive and negative effects on origin activity.
source: Our data suggest that transcription has both positive and negative effects on origin activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transcription depletes ORC/MCM from gene bodies but enriches them at TSSs.

claim: Active transcription removes ORC/MCM from transcribed gene bodies, which reduces their replication initiation capacity.
source: Actively transcribed gene bodies are depleted of ORC/MCM (Figure 2, Figure 3a). As reported in Drosophila (Powell et al., 2015), we propose that active transcription removes ORC/MCM from transcribed gene bodies, which reduces their replication initiation capacity.
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion of ORC/MCM from transcribed genes and supported by a cited study.

claim: The mechanism of transcription-mediated ORC/MCM removal is consistent with previous studies reporting that replication does not initiate within transcribed genes.
source: This mechanism is consistent with previous studies reporting that replication does not initiate within transcribed genes (Hamlin et al., 2010; Hyrien et al., 1995; Knott et al., 2009; Macheret and Halazonetis, 2018; Martin et al., 2011; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Active TSSs are regions of open chromatin structure characterized by DNase- or MNase hypersensitivity.
source: Active TSSs are regions of open chromatin structure characterized by DNase- or MNase hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromatin structure at active promoters.

claim: DNase or MNase hypersensitivity is a hallmark of Ma-IZs.
source: Such hypersensitivity is also a hallmark of Ma-IZs (Boulos et al., 2015; Papior et al., 2012) and preferred ORC binding sites (Miotto et al., 2016; Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Increased ORC binding at TSSs does not necessarily increase local initiation efficiency.
source: However, this increased ORC binding does not necessarily increase local initiation efficiency since the most efficient initiation sites identified by EdUseq-HU within early IZs are associated with poly(dA:dT) tracts, but not TSSs (Tubbs et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: MCMs are less enriched at TSSs than ORC, arguing against highly preferential origin licensing at TSSs.
source: Our finding that MCMs are less enriched at TSSs than ORC also argues against highly preferential origin licensing at TSSs.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing differential enrichment of ORC and MCM at TSSs.

claim: The preferred binding of ORC at TSSs does not result in increased MCM-DH loading specifically upstream of genes.
source: Furthermore, since MCMs are distributed fairly evenly upstream and downstream of transcribed gene bodies (Figure 3a), the preferred binding of ORC at TSSs does not result in increased MCM-DH loading specifically upstream of genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MCM levels are similar upstream and downstream of genes.

claim: IZs are enriched in the histone variant H2A.Z and in open chromatin marks typical of active or poised enhancers.
source: We previously reported that IZs are enriched in the histone variant H2A.Z and in open chromatin marks (H3K4me1, H3K27ac, DNAse HS sites) typical of active or poised enhancers (Petryk et al., 2016), which could potentially explain why IZs are more accessible to firing factors than flanking segments with comparable MCM-DH density.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study from the authors' group.

claim: Open chromatin marks at IZs could explain why IZs are more accessible to firing factors than flanking segments with comparable MCM-DH density.
source: We previously reported that IZs are enriched in the histone variant H2A.Z and in open chromatin marks (H3K4me1, H3K27ac, DNAse HS sites) typical of active or poised enhancers (Petryk et al., 2016), which could potentially explain why IZs are more accessible to firing factors than flanking segments with comparable MCM-DH density.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of IZ specification.

claim: H2A.Z recruits Suv420H1, which induces H4K20 dimethylation.
source: Recently, it was reported that H2A.Z recruits Suv420H1, which induces H4K20 dimethylation (Long et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: H4K20me2 interacts with the BAH domain of ORC1.
source: H4K20me2 interacts with the BAH domain of ORC1 (Beck et al., 2012a; Kuo et al., 2012; Vermeulen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The H2A.Z–H4K20me2–ORC1 axis supports a role for H2A.Z in ORC recruitment and origin licensing.
source: The H2A.Z–H4K20me2–ORC1 axis therefore supports a role for H2A.Z in ORC recruitment and origin licensing (Long et al., 2020; Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: H3.3/H2A.Z double variant–containing nucleosomes present at active promoters and other regulatory regions constitute a less stable nucleosome that is more easily displaced, resulting in nucleosome-free gaps.
source: Furthermore, H3.3/H2A.Z double variant–containing nucleosomes present at active promoters and other regulatory regions constitute a less stable nucleosome that is more easily displaced, resulting in nucleosome-free gaps (Jin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Nucleosome-free gaps associated with H3K4me2 are found at most binding sites for the origin-firing factor Treslin/MTBP.
source: Interestingly, nucleosome-free gaps associated with H3K4me2 are found at most binding sites for the origin-firing factor Treslin/MTBP, which may form looping interactions with distantly located MCM-DH to promote dispersed initiation within broad zones (Kumagai and Dunphy, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Treslin/MTBP may form looping interactions with distantly located MCM-DH to promote dispersed initiation within broad zones.
source: Interestingly, nucleosome-free gaps associated with H3K4me2 are found at most binding sites for the origin-firing factor Treslin/MTBP, which may form looping interactions with distantly located MCM-DH to promote dispersed initiation within broad zones (Kumagai and Dunphy, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Multiple open chromatin marks previously detected within IZs may promote not only origin licensing, but also origin firing.
source: These results provide novel insight into how multiple open chromatin marks previously detected within IZs may promote not only origin licensing, but also origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the various studies linking chromatin marks to both ORC recruitment and firing factor binding.

claim: H4K20 methylation has multiple functions in ensuring genome integrity, such as DNA replication, DNA repair, and chromatin compaction.
source: H4K20 methylation has multiple functions in ensuring genome integrity, such as DNA replication (Beck et al., 2012b; Long et al., 2020; Picard et al., 2014; Tardat et al., 2010), DNA repair, and chromatin compaction (Jørgensen et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2019; Shoaib et al., 2018), suggesting that the different functions are context-dependent and executed with different players.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The different functions of H4K20 methylation are context-dependent and executed with different players.
source: H4K20 methylation has multiple functions in ensuring genome integrity, such as DNA replication (Beck et al., 2012b; Long et al., 2020; Picard et al., 2014; Tardat et al., 2010), DNA repair, and chromatin compaction (Jørgensen et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2019; Shoaib et al., 2018), suggesting that the different functions are context-dependent and executed with different players.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple functions of H4K20 methylation.

claim: It is important to discriminate between H4K20me2, which is the most abundant H4K20 methylation state, and H4K20me3, which is more restricted.
source: However, it is important to discriminate between H4K20me2, which is the most abundant H4K20 methylation state, and H4K20me3, which is more restricted (Jørgensen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: H4K20me3 provides a platform to enhance licensing in late-replicating heterochromatin.
source: We previously demonstrated that H4K20me3 provides a platform to enhance licensing in late-replicating heterochromatin (Brustel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study from the authors' group.

claim: Replication licensing is functionally linked to H4K20me3 in a specific subset of late-replicating domains.
source: We functionally link replication licensing to H4K20me3 in a specific subset of late-replicating domains as we detect both elevated ORC and MCM levels when selecting for H4K20me3-enriched non-genic ASs and NRRs (Figures 5f and 6b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: It has been proposed that RT could simply result from the spatial distribution of potential origins upon S phase entry.
source: In higher eukaryotes, it has been proposed that RT could simply result from the spatial distribution of potential origins upon S phase entry.
evidence: This is a model proposed in the literature.

claim: The spatial distribution of potential origins has been derived from ORC or MCM-DH abundance, as well as from epigenetic mark profiles.
source: The latter distribution has been derived from ORC (Dellino et al., 2013; Miotto et al., 2016) or MCM-DH (Das et al., 2015; Hyrien, 2016) abundance, as well as from epigenetic mark profiles Gindin et al., 2014.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Miotto et al., 2016 performed computational simulations where stochastic initiations at experimentally mapped ORC binding sites allow to reproduce human RT profiles.
source: For example, Miotto et al., 2016 performed computational simulations where stochastic initiations at experimentally mapped ORC binding sites allow to reproduce human RT profiles.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: There is a convincing correlation of ORC density with RT.
source: Our data also indicate a convincing correlation of ORC density with RT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ChIP-seq and Repli-seq analyses.

claim: There is a weaker correlation of MCM-DH density with RT.
source: However, we observed a weaker correlation of MCM-DH density with RT, and a lack of correlation with RFD slope, suggesting that origin-firing probability, and therefore RT, is not solely regulated by MCM-DH density (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: There is a lack of correlation between MCM-DH density and RFD slope.
source: However, we observed a weaker correlation of MCM-DH density with RT, and a lack of correlation with RFD slope, suggesting that origin-firing probability, and therefore RT, is not solely regulated by MCM-DH density (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Origin-firing probability, and therefore RT, is not solely regulated by MCM-DH density.
source: However, we observed a weaker correlation of MCM-DH density with RT, and a lack of correlation with RFD slope, suggesting that origin-firing probability, and therefore RT, is not solely regulated by MCM-DH density (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between MCM density and RFD slope.

claim: All chromatin marks associated to open chromatin allowed very good predictions of RT profiles.
source: In fact, it was recently observed that all chromatin marks associated to open chromatin allowed very good predictions of RT profiles Gindin et al., 2014.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Open chromatin independently facilitates ORC binding in G1 phase and access of firing factors to MCM-DHs in S phase.
source: Since open chromatin independently facilitates ORC binding in G1 phase and access of firing factors to MCM-DHs in S phase, open chromatin marks and ORC density may both predict RT without implying a direct causal link between RT and ORC binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both open chromatin and ORC density correlate with RT.

claim: Open chromatin marks and ORC density may both predict RT without implying a direct causal link between RT and ORC binding.
source: Since open chromatin independently facilitates ORC binding in G1 phase and access of firing factors to MCM-DHs in S phase, open chromatin marks and ORC density may both predict RT without implying a direct causal link between RT and ORC binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both open chromatin and ORC density correlate with RT.

claim: Only the location of MCM-DHs associated with appropriate open chromatin marks to recruit firing factors is causative of RT.
source: Probably, only the location of MCM-DHs associated with appropriate open chromatin marks to recruit firing factors is causative of RT.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of RT determination.

claim: The spatio-temporal replication program can change during cellular differentiation.
source: The spatio-temporal replication program can change during cellular differentiation (Marchal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Early and late RTDs correspond to the more and less accessible compartments of the genome, respectively.
source: Comparison with chromatin conformation capture (Hi-C) data has shown that early and late RTDs correspond to the more and less accessible compartments of the genome, respectively (Ryba et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Sima et al. used the CRISPR-Cas9 technology to identify three separate, cis-acting elements that together control the early replication time of the pluripotency-associated Dppa2/4 domain in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
source: Recently, Sima et al. used the CRISPR-Cas9 technology to identify three separate, cis-acting elements that together control the early replication time of the pluripotency-associated Dppa2/4 domain in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) Sima et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Early replication control elements (ERCEs) are enriched in CTCF-independent Hi-C interactions and active epigenetic marks previously observed at OK-seq IZs.
source: Strikingly, these early replication control elements (ERCEs) are enriched in CTCF-independent Hi-C interactions and active epigenetic marks (DNase1 HS, p300, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3) previously observed at OK-seq IZs (Petryk et al., 2018; Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The three ERCEs of the Dppa2/4 domain fall within IZs.
source: By mining mESC OK-seq data (Petryk et al., 2018), we found that the three ERCEs of the Dppa2/4 domain indeed fall within IZs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The aggregate 1835 ERCEs predicted genome-wide by Sima et al. from epigenetic profiles of mESCs shows a significant, positive RFD shift indicative of efficient replication initiation.
source: Furthermore, the aggregate 1835 ERCEs predicted genome-wide by Sima et al., from epigenetic profiles of mESCs, shows a significant, positive RFD shift indicative of efficient replication initiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The positive RFD shift at ERCEs is confirmed in proliferating PHA-stimulated primary splenic B cells.
source: This finding is confirmed in proliferating PHA-stimulated primary splenic B cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c), attesting to the general validity of these observations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: A higher ORC/MCM density is not a distinguishing feature of IZs from the rest of the genome.
source: Since our data suggest that a higher ORC/MCM density is not a distinguishing feature of IZs from the rest of the genome, IZ specification cannot solely occur at the origin-licensing step.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density does not distinguish IZs from other regions of similar RT.

claim: IZ specification cannot solely occur at the origin-licensing step.
source: Since our data suggest that a higher ORC/MCM density is not a distinguishing feature of IZs from the rest of the genome, IZ specification cannot solely occur at the origin-licensing step.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC/MCM density does not distinguish IZs from other regions of similar RT.

claim: Open and dynamic chromatin structures found at Ma-IZs and ERCEs might not only facilitate origin licensing in G1 but also promote chromatin binding of limiting firing factors during S phase.
source: Open and dynamic chromatin structures found at Ma-IZs and ERCEs (Petryk et al., 2016; Sima et al., 2019) might not only facilitate origin licensing in G1 but also promote chromatin binding of limiting firing factors during S phase (Boos and Ferreira, 2019; Krude et al., 1997; Kumagai and Dunphy, 2020).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by cited studies.

claim: In human cells most of the genome, except transcribed genes, is licensed for replication during the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Our mapping of ORC and MCM complexes shows that in human cells most of the genome, except transcribed genes, is licensed for replication during the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the widespread distribution of ORC/MCM throughout the genome except in transcribed genes.

claim: Only a fraction of MCM-DHs is selected for initiation during S phase.
source: ORC/MCM are more enriched in early than in late RTDs (Figure 7a) but only a fraction of MCM-DHs is selected for initiation during S phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that not all licensed origins fire.

claim: Open chromatin marks define efficient Ma-IZs, often but not always circumscribed by active genes.
source: Open chromatin marks define efficient Ma-IZs, often but not always circumscribed by active genes (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analyses of IZs in relation to transcription and chromatin marks.

claim: Open chromatin marks at Ma-IZs may favor origin licensing in G1 but also binding of origin firing factors in S phase.
source: Such marks may favor origin licensing in G1 but also binding of origin firing factors in S phase.

claim: Once forks emanate from Ma-IZs within an RTD, the omnipresence of MCM-DHs allows a cascade of replication initiation to take place dispersively between IZs.
